instructions:
Voice Affect: calm, curious and clear.
Tone: conversational mathematical teaching for a bright sixteen-year-old.
Pacing: steady and unhurried; pause briefly around numbers and definitions.
Pronunciation: say Hex clearly; read symbols as the supplied words.
Delivery: no imitation of any person or branded presentation style.

clips.text: Blue wants a chain from the top to the bottom. Red wants a chain from the left to the right. They take turns claiming empty cells. The question is not just who wins, but how cheaply Blue can force a win.

Two cells connect when they share an edge. An interior hexagon has six neighbours. We use ordinary alternating play, Blue first, with no swap rule. A strategy must work against every legal reply, not just a helpful opponent.
Start with this two by two board. Blue takes the upper-right cell. It touches the top, and it is adjacent to both cells on the bottom. Blue now has two possible ways to complete a connection.

If Red takes the lower-left cell, Blue takes the lower-right. If Red takes the lower-right, Blue takes the lower-left. A reply somewhere else also leaves a winning move. Red cannot occupy both threats in one turn.

Notice what Blue did not need: a path chosen before Red moved. Blue chose the final route after seeing the reply. That difference between a fixed route and an adaptive strategy will matter on the larger board.
Move to five by five. Any top-to-bottom path must visit all five rows, so it needs at least five cells. But a geometric path on an empty board is not yet a path Blue can force against Red.

There are two different costs. Count the cells in the final connecting path, or count every stone Blue placed. We call the best forced path cost lambda, and the best forced stone cost delta. On five by five, they differ.

Here is an actual branch of the certified five-by-five strategy. Blue opens in the centre. We will follow all twenty-three moves. Odd move numbers are Blue, even numbers Red. For this branch, Red delays the connection as long as possible.

The stones spread across the board. A stone that is not on the eventual winning route can still matter: it may create another threat or answer a defence. Keep watching which cells remain available as the players alternate.

Now the last seven moves complete the position. Blue first connects on move twenty-three. This is one legal game from the strategy, not the universal proof by itself. The proof must account for Red's other possible replies too.

Trace this winning route. Start in the top-right cell, move down-left, then down, across, down, and down-left to the bottom. Count the cells: one, two, three, four, five, six. That is the shortest Blue connection here.

But Blue has placed twelve stones. Six are on this shortest path, and six are elsewhere. This one position makes the distinction visible: path length six does not mean Blue won on the sixth Blue move.

The full certificate proves that Blue can always produce a path of at most six cells. Separate Red certificates prevent a path of at most five after every opening. Together, these two directions establish lambda of five equals six.

A different pair of bounds establishes delta of five equals seven. Red can stop a win made with six Blue stones, while another Blue strategy wins using at most seven. Our twelve-stone illustration is not a stone-minimising strategy.

Why can a seemingly convincing argument miss the shorter path? Suppose you first commit to one route. Red only needs one cell on that route to block it. That proves the chosen route is vulnerable, not that every adaptive strategy fails.

Return to the tiny board. Either bottom cell blocks one proposed route, but leaves the other. The winning route depends on Red's move. This is the quantifier order: Blue chooses a strategy, Red replies, and the route can then adapt.

A game tree expresses that order. At a Blue turn, one successful move is enough. At a Red turn, every legal reply must be handled. A single successful branch is evidence for a possibility; a strategy covers the whole relevant tree.

The search writes down a proposed move at each position it needs. An independent checker reads those moves and examines the opponent's replies. It does not assume that the search's shortcuts were safe. It checks the proposed strategy itself.

For each position, the checker verifies that the prescribed move is legal. Then it tries every empty cell as the opponent's reply and continues. Terminal connections are checked on the actual occupied cells. This turns a strategy table into a replayable certificate.

The search can also view the problem as a family of target sets. On five by five, there are one hundred and six inclusion-minimal connecting cell sets of size at most six. Red kills a target by occupying any of its cells.

The certified central six-cell strategy was replayed through one hundred and six thousand, eight hundred and twenty-six checked positions. This counter summarises that retained replay. It is not a live search, and the number counts positions where a certified move was tested.

There is one rule detail to settle. Under the continued-play definition, a long Blue connection does not finish the short-path task. Play may continue until Blue makes a sufficiently short path. Under the strict definition, the first connection ends the game.

The five-by-five value is six under both readings. A separate strict certificate handles the first-connection rule. So the correction is not explained away by choosing a different stopping convention. The two definitions could still differ on larger boards.

On six by six, the stone budget is exactly ten. Red can prevent a connection using nine or fewer Blue stones after every opening. A certified Blue strategy, opening at row three, column four, succeeds with at most ten.

Ten Blue moves mean at most nineteen moves altogether: Blue makes ten, and Red moves in the nine gaps. The lower-bound defence shows why fewer Blue stones cannot be guaranteed. This is a stone-budget statement, not a path-length statement.
For path length on six by six, the certified statement is a lower bound of eight. Every one of the thirty-six possible openings has a Red certificate stopping all Blue paths of seven cells or fewer.

Those thirty-six seven-cell defence certificates account for twenty-two million, seven hundred and eighty thousand, and ninety-seven checked positions. Their completed replay records were recovered and reconciled. This video does not claim that the large searches were rerun during production.

A separate exhaustive search found a Blue strategy for a path of at most eight cells. But that upper bound has no independently replayed certificate. We therefore keep it visibly labelled search-only, rather than presenting an exact certified value of eight.

Nor does that search settle the strict six-by-six value. The retained bounds for the first-connection reading are eight through ten. On five by five both readings are resolved; on six by six an exact strict value is not claimed.

Campbell introduced these measures and conjectured the small-board values in two thousand and four. The certified five-by-five path value is six rather than the proposed seven. It also contradicts the seven claimed in the two thousand and twenty-six Casco, Pacifico and Sanhueza preprint.

The six-by-six stone value ten contradicts the proposed nine. But it agrees with an earlier nineteen-move estimate from H Z Y's KataHex work in two thousand and twenty-four. That prior estimate deserves credit; the new evidence is the replayable proof.

The verification includes corrupted certificates that the checkers reject, as well as valid controls. There is no Lean formalisation. Confidence is high for the certified claims, conditional on the written game reduction and independent checker, and more limited for the unreplayed search result.

The lesson is threefold. A strategy can change its route. A short final path can require extra stones. And a search result becomes stronger evidence when a separate checker verifies the strategy against every possible defence.

The certified results are six for the five-by-five path, seven for its stone budget, ten for the six-by-six stone budget, and at least eight for its path. Larger boards and the exact strict six-by-six value remain outside these conclusions.

The paper, strategy evidence and editable animation accompany this video. The prior-work search was bounded, so originality is stated with moderate confidence. The diagrams replay retained examples and explain the checking logic. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
